plan: [In a 3-player third-price auction the winner pays the lowest bid, so my bid only affects whether I win (unless it becomes the minimum). Opponents' expected minimum value ≈49/3 ≈16.33. My private value is 36, well above that, so winning is profitable in expectation. To maximize long-run profit, I should ensure winning when profitable by bidding high enough to beat others. I'll place the maximum reasonable bid to secure the win and pay their minimum.]

[I model the two opponents as symmetric, bidding their values (uniform 0–49). If I bid b, P(win)=(b/49)^2 and conditional expected payment = b/3, so expected payoff ∝ b^2(8 − b/3). Maximizing 8b^2 − b^3/3 gives optimum b=16. Thus I overbid my private value (8) to maximize expected long-run profit given symmetric opponents.]

[Because the winner pays the lowest of the three bids, my own bid only affects whether I win, not the payment when I am highest. With v=44, bidding very high (49) wins almost always and yields expected profit = 44 − E[min(other two)] ≈ 44 − 49/3 > 0. The small chance both opponents exceed 44 could produce a loss, but that event is rare. Maximizing long-run profit here means bidding the maximum to capture many profitable wins where the third-price (minimum) is well below 44.]
